title: Lamrim: the round of suffering
hook: the faults of samsara, seen plainly

segments.voice: Yesterday on the stages of the path, karma: actions have results, and the seeds are small. Your line was small grows large. Did one small good deed get done? Day one thousand two hundred ninety-two.

The dishwasher clicks off. Everything comes out clean and goes back in the cupboard. By dinner the sink is full again, and the whole thing starts over. Nobody did anything wrong. That's just how dishes work. Now stretch that out. The craving that gets fed and comes back hungrier. The same argument with the same person, in nearly the same words, one more time. A new phone, thrilling on Monday and ordinary by the weekend. The lamrim, the stages of the path, asks the student to stop at this point and look at the whole machine, plainly, without flinching. Today, the round of suffering.
screen: `THE SINK FILLS AGAIN.` → `THE SAME ARGUMENT, AGAIN.` → `LOOK AT THE WHOLE MACHINE.`

segments.voice: First, the name for the machine. Samsara, in Sanskrit, usually translated as wandering on. Tibetans call it khorwa, usually translated as circling. In this teaching it means the round of birth, death and birth again, driven by craving and confusion, life after life. Second, the faults. The lamrim texts don't stay vague here. They lay out what's wrong with the circle in plain terms. Nothing in it stays certain: friends become strangers, the high fall low, fortunes turn. Nothing in it satisfies for long: the more you drink of it, the thirstier you get. And it keeps happening, over and over, with no natural end in sight. Third, a picture from the older suttas. In one discourse in the Samyutta Nikaya, the Buddha asks his monks which is greater: the tears they have shed while wandering on through this long round, weeping over what they lost and what they couldn't have, or the water in the four great oceans. The answer in the text is the tears. It's meant to land like cold water on the face. Fourth, why look at all this. It can sound gloomy. Tibetan teachers explain it differently: you can't want to leave a place you haven't seen clearly. Seeing the round plainly gives rise to what they call renunciation, the honest wish to be free. That isn't hatred of life. Lunch is still good. A friend's laugh is still good. What the student turns away from is the circling itself, the getting caught again and again. Yesterday was karma, the engine. Today is the road it runs on. Tomorrow the path offers somewhere to turn.
screen: `SAMSARA: WANDERING ON, CIRCLING.` · `NO CERTAINTY, NO LASTING SATISFACTION.` · `MORE TEARS THAN THE FOUR OCEANS.` · `SEEING IT PLAINLY: THE WISH TO BE FREE.` · then, large: `ROUND AND ROUND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name one cycle you repeat. Sit comfortably and let a few breaths come and go. Then let one loop in your life come to mind. Checking the phone. The same worry at three in the morning. The same apology. Don't judge it and don't fix it yet. Just trace it once around: what starts it, what feeds it, what it promises, and how it ends up back where it began. Then give it a short, plain name. When you have the name, rest with the breath, which also goes round and round, and asks nothing of you. The bell holds the time.
Lamrim. The stages of the path. Today's stage: seeing samsara, the round of suffering, plainly enough to want out. Today's word.
Your line: round and round. Today, when the loop you named starts up, say its name quietly to yourself. Just catching it once counts. Day one thousand two hundred ninety-two.

howItsDone: In the Tibetan stages-of-the-path teaching, students reflect on the faults of samsara so that renunciation, the wish to be free of the round, grows strong before they turn to the later stages.

pairs: wandering on, the round of rebirth
less water than the tears shed
the honest wish to be free

myth: seeing the faults of samsara means hating life
teachers say it's the circling the student turns from, not friends, laughter or lunch.
in a sutta, the Buddha compares tears shed while wandering on to the four great oceans
the text says the tears are more.
the lamrim keeps the faults of samsara vague
it names them plainly: no certainty, no lasting satisfaction, and it keeps happening.

fork.setup: you've noticed the same loop in your life for the hundredth time. what does this stage of the lamrim ask of you first?
options: look at it plainly, all the way around.
fork.reveal: the teaching asks for clear seeing first. teachers say the wish to be free grows from seeing the round plainly, not from shame.

original.note: Sanskrit: samsara, the round of birth and death; in Tibetan, khorwa (འཁོར་བ), circling.

trapdoor: what you thought: samsara is just a fancy word for a hard life.
what it means: the whole round of birth, death and rebirth, driven by craving and confusion, seen as having no lasting rest in it.
what a scholar hears: in the lamrim, seeing these faults is the ground for renunciation, the wish for freedom that the later stages build on.
recall: treasure: a teaching hidden on purpose

notes: Samsara glossed 'usually translated as wandering on'; Tibetan 'khor ba glossed 'circling'. Confirm both glosses and the Tibetan spelling in the original game.
The faults of samsara are given loosely (uncertainty, no satisfaction, repetition) without a count; Tsongkhapa's list of faults is fuller. Confirm the paraphrase is fair.
SN 15.3: the tears versus the water of the four great oceans, paraphrased. Confirm the reference.
Renunciation described as 'not hatred of life': confirm this framing matches how Tibetan teachers present it.
